title: Logical Operators
body:
`not`, `and`, `or`: the three operators that combine [[Boolean]] values, and the reason a
[[Conditional]] can test more than one thing at once.

```python
if age >= 18 and has_id:
    ...
if not logged_in or session_expired:
    ...
```

| Operator | True when |
|---|---|
| `not a` | `a` is False |
| `a and b` | both are True |
| `a or b` | at least one is True |

**Precedence is `not`, then `and`, then `or`**, so `a or b and c` means `a or (b and c)`.
Parenthesise anything you would have to think about; that is a [[Style Conventions|style]]
argument as much as a correctness one.

## Short-circuit evaluation

**Python stops as soon as the answer is decided.** In `a and b`, if `a` is False then `b` is
never evaluated, because the result cannot change. Same for `a or b` when `a` is True.

That is not a performance footnote, it is a technique. It is what makes this safe:

```python
if count != 0 and total / count > 10:     # the division never runs when count is 0
```

Reverse the two halves and it crashes. The guard has to come first, and it works only because of
short-circuiting.

## The same algebra one course later

`and`, `or`, and `not` are AND, OR, and NOT from [[Boolean Algebra]] in
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]], where they are gates rather than keywords, and De Morgan's laws apply
here exactly as they do there:

```python
not (a and b)   ==   (not a) or (not b)
not (a or b)    ==   (not a) and (not b)
```

Useful immediately: they are how you simplify a condition you have accidentally written
inside-out. [[Systems of Logic]] is the same structure again as formal logic.
